data.title: Who is buying cards for major Chinese manufacturers?
data.description:
Author: Sleepy

Several data center financing deals in Southeast Asia have run into trouble.

Bridge Data Centres is expanding its Malaysian loan to $6.6 billion, with some lenders demanding additional due diligence. Bridge is a Bain Capital firm located in its MY06 campus in Johor, with ByteDance as its main tenant.

Bridge Data Centres is expanding its Malaysian loan to $6.6 billion, with some lenders demanding additional due diligence ...>

DayOne's data center campus in Nusajaya, Johor, Malaysia

Image source: DayOne

The companies involved fall into two categories.

DayOne and Bridge are data center operators responsible for building data centers, providing power, and renting out server racks.

DayOne and Bridge are data center operators responsible for building data centers, providing power, and renting out server racks.

DayOne and Bridge are data center operators responsible for building data centers, providing power, and renting out server racks.

Bridge is backed by Bain Capital, and its connection to China stems from Chindata. Bain merged Bridge into Chindata in 2019, privatized Chindata in 2023, and subsequently sold its China business to a consortium led by Dongyangguang for approximately $4 billion, retaining only its overseas operations. Drew Chen, who became co-CEO of Bridge this November, is a founding member of Bain's Asian private equity team. Bridge's tenants are also changing. In February of this year, Bridge informed its lenders that the 68.4 megawatts originally allocated to Megaspeed had been transferred to Zenlayer. Zenlayer, headquartered in Los Angeles, is considered a US company under the new regulations, but its founder, Joe Zhu, was formerly a senior vice president at ChinaCache. The company has teams in Shanghai, Hangzhou, and Beijing, and its Series B funding was led by Guangyuan Capital. Guangyuan Capital, spun out of the state-owned enterprise China Everbright, also appeared in DayOne's Series C investors. DayOne is the overseas business spun off from GDS Holdings. According to the prospectus, GDS gradually retreated to a minority shareholder position, converting its loans to DayOne into shares, ceasing consolidation by the end of 2024, and terminating trademark licensing and customer referrals by the end of 2025. In January of this year, DayOne spent $385 million to repurchase a portion of GDS's shares, reducing GDS's stake to 19.4%. After GDS's withdrawal, three other companies held similar stakes. At the time of the prospectus submission, the top four shareholders were Coatue and Hillhouse Capital (19.5% each), GDS (19.4%), and Zhongfang Capital (15.6%). Hillhouse Capital has been a shareholder since its Series A round. When Wanguo Securities announced its Series A round in March 2024, the listed investors included Hillhouse Capital and its real asset platform Rava Partners, as well as Boyu Capital and other institutions. Hillhouse's shares are currently pledged to a group of lenders, and DayOne's CFO worked at Hillhouse from 2023 to 2026. Zhongfang Capital is one of the largest shareholders. According to the prospectus, its four holding entities subscribed for approximately US$1.16 billion in total, with the US$210 million investment in the Series A round being the largest single investment in that round. This shareholder's office is in Taipei, and its controlling shareholder is Chen Zhuwang. He is the eldest grandson of Wang Yung-ching and the nephew of Wang Xuehong. He joined VIA Technologies in 1996 and served as CEO of VIA China. The board of directors includes representatives from both VIA Technologies and Alibaba. VIA Technologies founder Huang Wei remains a director, holding approximately 3.5% of the stock options. Andy Okada is the president of the SoftBank-Alibaba joint venture and also the CEO of Alibaba Japan. The chairman and CEO are from the Temasek Group. Chairman Lim Ah Doo served on the board of ST Telemedia and its subsidiary STT GDC for over a decade, while CEO Jamie Khoo was a senior finance executive at ST Telemedia before joining VIA Technologies. ST Telemedia is a Temasek subsidiary and still held approximately 29% of VIA Technologies' Class A shares as of the end of March this year. Alejandro Aguzín, a new director this year, served as CEO of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange from 2021 to 2024, and prior to that, as CEO of JPMorgan Chase Asia Pacific. Revenue primarily comes from one client. The prospectus states that in 2025, 69.4% of revenue will come from "a technology company with a leading short video platform," whose contracted capacity has increased from 64 MW to 838 MW. The prospectus also states that two of the company's existing clients are on the Pentagon's list of "Chinese military enterprises." Tencent was added to this list in January 2025, and Alibaba in June of this year. Another type of company that comes forward is Neocloud, which buys its own chips, builds its own clusters, and then rents out its computing power to large companies on an hourly basis. The borrower of the frozen loan mentioned at the beginning, Aolani, is one such company. Aolani has been renting H100 servers to ByteDance in Malaysia since February 2025, and this year it prepared approximately 36,000 B200 servers for ByteDance. Its holding company is registered in the Cayman Islands, and its early investor is Singapore's K3 Ventures. K3's founder, Guo Mengxiong, is the grandson of Robert Kuok, and according to his resume disclosed in companies such as TVS Motor, he is also a director of ByteDance's Singapore entity. Aolani's servers are purchased from Aivres. Aivres was formerly Inspur Systems, Inspur's US subsidiary, and was renamed in 2023. Financial reports and US court documents show that Aivres is indirectly wholly owned by Inspur Information through Hong Kong's KAYTUS Holdings and the British Virgin Islands' KAYTUS Group. According to The New York Times, from April 2024 to February of this year, Aivres shipped at least $5.6 billion worth of servers to Southeast Asia. Inspur Group was added to the Entity List in March 2023, and Inspur Information was added last March; Aivres itself is not on the list. The US "50% related-party rule" is currently suspended until January 10th of next year. Once the rule is reinstated, subsidiaries of companies listed with more than half their shares will be subject to control, including Aivres, which is 100% owned by Inspur Information. GMI Cloud is also known as NeoCloud. Founder Ye Weiyan is the son of Ye Jiawen, co-founder of Realtek Semiconductor. The company initially focused on Bitcoin computing power, and its Series A investors included the Thai energy group Banpu. The Thai data center it used to buy chips for Tencent was hosted by STT GDC's Thai joint venture. STT GDC originally belonged to ST Telemedia, but was acquired by KKR and Singtel from Temasek in September of this year. The Thai joint venture's 51% stake is held by Frasers Property, a subsidiary of the Su Xuming family's TCC Group. Bridge replaced Megaspeed, which is backed by Alibaba. Alibaba was Megaspeed's founding anchor customer. In June 2024, Alibaba's Singapore subsidiary Apex lent money to Megaspeed's Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, with Speedmatrix pledging its entire business to Apex. According to The New York Times, most of Speedmatrix's chips also come from Aivres, running for Alibaba in YTL's Johor data center. YTL calls this claim "speculation and unfounded." YTL, mentioned above, was NVIDIA's earliest partner in Malaysia. In December 2023, Jensen Huang visited Kuala Lumpur and announced an AI infrastructure collaboration with YTL. YTL now claims that its GPU business has only one 10-megawatt NVIDIA DGX Cloud project, fully funded by NVIDIA; the rest are managed and it does not provide GPU services to Chinese customers. There is another data center in Johor that was not mentioned in this report. Bitdeer, founded by Bitmain founder Jihan Wu, has a data center called A201 there, where they purchased over 100 racks of GB300 computing power, scheduled to be powered on early next year. Bitdeer says that over 70% of the capacity has already been committed by customers, with five-year contracts exceeding $1.7 billion, and the money for the cards mainly comes from customer prepayments. According to the New York Times, the computing power of this data center was planned to be sold to a Chinese tech giant. After the new regulations were introduced, brokerage firm StoneX estimated that there was a 25% chance that A201 would not be sold. The companies that lent them the money to buy the cards were mostly borrowed. Banks lent money to operators to buy chips, with the chips used as collateral, and long-term leases from large manufacturers serving as the source of repayment. Aolani's $480 million loan was calculated based on a debt service coverage ratio of 1.15. According to Natixis, syndicated loans for ASEAN data centers have totaled approximately US$48 billion since 2023. From major companies to operators, Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase have been involved in almost every stage.

In 2025, DayOne held a RM15 billion syndicated loan signing ceremony with several banksImage source: UOB

In September of this year, they led a $29.6 billion loan to ByteDance, unsecured, SOFR plus 68 basis points.

This September, they led a $29.6 billion loan to ByteDance, unsecured, SOFR plus 68 basis points.

For Bridge's $2.8 billion loan last year, each of them contributed approximately $120 million. This data center serves both ByteDance and has a service contract with Megaspeed. Bain Capital also handled the sale of at least 40% of Bridge's equity in April of this year. Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan Chase were the lead underwriters for DayOne's IPO, with Citigroup also involved; JPMorgan Chase is also the depositary bank for its American Depositary Shares. Singaporean banks were responsible for lead management and distribution. DBS was the lead underwriter for Aolani's loan, and three Singaporean banks were involved in DayOne's approximately $3.7 billion loan in Johor this October. Chinese banks have always been present; the closer they are to ByteDance, the more money they contribute. Of ByteDance's $29.6 billion loan, 15 Chinese banks contributed $18.9 billion, accounting for 64%. Further down the chain, at the telecom operator level, there are also Chinese banks. The $2.8 billion loan to Bridge includes Bank of China and China Minsheng Bank, and Industrial Bank also stated in a press release that it was the lead bank for one of Bridge's overseas syndicated loans. For Epoch Digital's data center in Johor, a $488 million loan was led by Bank of China and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB). The AIIB's project page states that the first phase of 60 megawatts was entirely contracted to ByteDance's BytePlus. For a data center in Rayong, Thailand, where ByteDance is the main tenant, the first phase loan was led by China Merchants Bank. Nvidia is also helping these companies borrow money, in a way that involves providing guarantees. For GMI Cloud's GPU loan in Taiwan, Nvidia promised to lease idle computing power at an agreed price for six years, while taking half of the revenue GMI earns from other customers. For Zankore's $3.1 billion loan in Indonesia, Nvidia provided revenue sharing and credit support. These guarantees, as far as we can see, have all been given to projects whose clients are not Chinese companies. Nvidia's equity investments are not so clearly defined. It is a shareholder of GMI and also of the UK-based neocloud Nscale, participating in several rounds of Nscale's financing since September 2025. In Nscale's IPO filing this year, it also committed to subscribing to $2 billion in convertible bonds. Of Nscale's $33 million in revenue in 2025, approximately 73% came from ByteDance's Singapore subsidiary, Spring. This proportion dropped to 52% in the first half of this year, and Nscale expects it to fall below 20% for the full year. The new regulations, effective November 16th, are based on the customer's headquarters. Regardless of the country where a data center is located, if it provides more than 12 million TPPs of computing power (approximately 750 H100 servers) to a company headquartered in or ultimately with a parent company in China, or if Chinese customers account for more than half of the total computing power, a license is required to supply chips. Existing data centers must obtain licenses within 90 days, with a deadline of February 17, 2027. This rule could have been much more lenient. Reportedly, Commerce Secretary Lutnick's original version only addressed future shipments, requiring only reporting for Chinese customers training models, and had a higher threshold. That version would have allowed Bitdeer's A201, and Lutnick's Cantor Fitzgerald was the sales agent for Bitdeer's potential $1 billion share issuance. Between Cantor and Bitdeer lies stablecoin giant Tether. Cantor acquired approximately 5% of Tether's shares in 2024. In May of the same year, Tether invested $100 million in Bitdeer, with Cantor also acting as the placement agent for that transaction. By June of this year, Tether held approximately 19.7% of Bitdeer's Class A shares. After Lutnick transferred his Cantor shares to a trust for his children, Tether provided a loan to that trust, with collateral including more than half of Cantor's equity. The final version released was stricter. According to Politico, it was pushed by Treasury Secretary Bessant, with Rubio on his side. Bessant stated that the Treasury Department had been advocating for Megaspeed to be added to the Entity List for months, but "the pen is in the hands of the Commerce Department." A week after the new rules were released, on November 23, seven companies, including Megaspeed, Speedmatrix, and Alibaba's Apex, were added to the Entity List. There are three details in the rules specifically targeting the practice of having someone else purchase the cards on their behalf. The first point concerns "indirect buyers." The rule states that the 2023 regulation, as determined by headquarters, "never applies only" to the direct recipient. Chinese companies, whether direct or indirect buyers in a transaction, or the sole or primary user of a data center, are also subject to this regulation. Large companies that prepay rent or lend money to operators may be considered indirect buyers. The second point concerns retroactive application. Law firm Paul Weiss interprets this as BIS believing that this regulation has been in effect since November 2023, and transactions from the past three years may constitute violations, thus encouraging companies to proactively disclose such information. The third point concerns exemptions for referral systems. Computing power used solely for recommendation systems does not require a license, provided that the data center reports the names of Chinese clients, their computing power usage, and the due diligence conducted to the BIS. This information is then forwarded to the End-User Review Committee, which determines the Entity List. The rules gave 90 days, and the banks began taking action within a week. The banks acted so quickly because financing itself may be illegal. Section 10 of the U.S. Export Administration Regulations (Export Administration Regulations) lists "financing" as a prohibited activity; regardless of whether one is a U.S. citizen or not, knowingly providing financing in violation of regulations can lead to prosecution. In October 2024, the BIS issued compliance guidelines specifically to financial institutions, with civil penalties up to twice the transaction amount. Applied Materials was fined $252.5 million in February of this year under this standard. We found no precedent for BIS to punish banks based on this injunction. However, once the rule is applied retroactively, banks will need to re-examine not only new loans but also funds already disbursed. Bloomberg also mentioned that some older loans may be deemed to have violated loan terms.

DBS signage outside the DBS building in Singapore

Image source: DBS

On November 18th, Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase added a clause to their Bridge loans stating that violations of US export controls would constitute default. This decision came from the two banks' New York headquarters.

Regional banks like DBS earn lead generation and distribution fees, provided they can sell the loans and transfer the risk.

The market for taking over loans was already tight this year. HSBC and Deutsche Bank were both transferring risk for data center loans, and Barclays was seeking insurance for over $10 billion in AI infrastructure credit, with insurance companies' underwriting capacity "nearly exhausted." After the new regulations, a risk transfer of approximately $1 billion by UOB also slowed down. A Singaporean syndicated banker interviewed by IFR said that no one was willing to commit even $100 million until the rules were clear. Interest rates also varied significantly. ByteDance borrowed its own money at SOFR plus 68 basis points; AirTrunk's general data center loan in Malaysia was at SOFR plus 225 basis points; Zankore's GPU loan customer was a US fintech company, backed by Nvidia, at SOFR plus 330 basis points. The same GMI, with Nvidia backing its loan in Taiwan, had an interest rate of approximately 3.43%. The expected yield on Tencent's chip purchase in Thailand is in the teens, but the draft term sheet states that Tencent must repay the loan in full early if it is added to the US restricted list. Smaller neoclouds in the US without credit ratings borrow at approximately SOFR plus 800 to 900 basis points. Tencent itself has a Moody's A1 and S&P A+ rating, yet the pricing for GPU loans using Tencent as a tenant is similar to that of small, unrated US companies. The three companies' situations differ: they acquire computing power overseas in different ways, and the impact they face is also different. ByteDance has the largest footprint. According to SemiAnalysis estimates, ByteDance alone uses about one-fifth of the computing power delivered in China. According to the Straits Times, citing industry and government sources, ByteDance leases about 90% of the computing capacity in Johor, mostly CPUs, running services like TikTok, which largely qualify for exemptions for recommendation systems. The AI ​​portion cannot qualify; the 60 megawatts signed with BytePlus are for enterprise AI cloud, and Aolani's 36,000 B200 chips are for training. This portion of computing power is constrained, and ByteDance lacks its own chips to fill the gap. It is the only major Chinese platform without commercially available AI acceleration chips. According to LatePost, ByteDance's AI chip was taped out this year, but its performance did not meet standards, and Shi Yunfeng, who was in charge of the AI ​​chip, has resigned. ByteDance's confidence comes from its financial resources; nearly two-thirds of its $29.6 billion loan came from Chinese banks, making it the most capable of bearing the risk itself among the three. Besides acting as a tenant, Alibaba also directly lent money to telecom operators through Apex, using the operators' entire business as collateral. According to the new regulations' definition of "indirect buyer," this is precisely the practice most easily traced. Apex also became the first subsidiary of the three major companies to be added to the Entity List. However, Alibaba has not scaled back its overseas operations. The day after the new regulations were released, Alibaba Cloud announced in Hong Kong that it would build new data centers in nine locations within a year, including Malaysia and Brazil, both of which are among the five countries specifically mentioned in the new regulations where shipments require licenses. Alibaba is still betting on Pingtouge (a chip manufacturer). Wu Yongming stated in a conference call that Pingtouge chips can support ultra-large-scale training, and the new generation Zhenwu V900 will enter mass production in the first quarter of next year. Morgan Stanley estimates that Alibaba wants to increase the proportion of its self-developed chips in its computing power from over 10% to 40-50%. [Image caption: Inside Tencent's Gui'an Qixing Data Center in Guizhou] [Image source: Cailian Press] [Image caption: Tencent's pressure lies in cash.] It operates on a prepayment model. In the third quarter, Tencent's free cash flow was negative 69.1 billion yuan. The company stated that excluding prepayments for computing power, it was positive 16.9 billion yuan, meaning approximately 86 billion yuan was prepaid in one quarter. At the end of June, Tencent had net cash of 58.2 billion yuan, which turned into net debt of 13.7 billion yuan by the end of September. The largest prepayment went to Oracle. For five years, approximately 100,000 Nvidia chips were placed in Oracle's Southeast Asian data centers, a contract worth approximately $7 billion, with Tencent prepaying about 30%. According to the Financial Times, after US officials "expressed concerns," Oracle canceled the agreement in early November. One of Oracle's data centers in Southeast Asia was leased from DayOne. According to Bloomberg, Oracle became the sole tenant of DayOne's Nongsa campus in Batam, Indonesia, in 2025. Oracle also holds a 15% stake in TikTok's US joint venture and is its security partner. Tencent also has a presence in Japan and Australia that has run into problems. Datasection, listed in Tokyo, derives 90.7% of its revenue in fiscal year 2026 from a company called NowNaw Japan. According to a Financial Times report last December, NowNaw's end customer is Tencent, involving contracts exceeding $1.2 billion in Tokyo and Sydney. Tencent responded at the time that its use of cloud services complies with applicable laws. In August of this year, an additional order worth 79.86 billion yen was cancelled. On November 16th, Datasection further slashed its revenue forecast for the current fiscal year from 162.2 billion yen to 17.3 billion yen. The landlord of the Sydney data center terminated the lease after months of dragging out negotiations to switch from B200 to B300. Tracing back the companies that bought the cards, most of the names that can be found are familiar faces. Taiwanese and Southeast Asian Chinese family capital, along with Singaporean state capital, have been acting as intermediaries between China and the West for decades, involved in manufacturing, real estate, and ports, with money and goods passing through their hands. AI computing power is the newest category in this business. Chinese manufacturers have demand, and the West has chips and dollar loans. They offer a company identity acceptable to both sides, and a piece of land where electricity can be connected. This business requires choosing sides periodically. In November 1989, Wang Yung-ching visited mainland China for the first time and subsequently proposed building an integrated upstream, midstream, and downstream petrochemical zone in Haicang, Xiamen, known as "Project 901." The news caused considerable controversy in Taiwan, with Taipei intervening to retain the project, offering tax breaks and a $1.5 billion water supply facility, while also lowering land and water prices. In August 1991, Wang Yung-ching accepted the Yunlin Mailiao proposal, which later became the Sixth Naphtha Cracking Plant. In November 1992, he held a press conference announcing the suspension of the Haicang project. More than thirty years later, his eldest grandson's Zhongfang Capital became DayOne's fourth-largest shareholder.

The signing ceremony of the investment cooperation agreement between Microsoft and G42 in 2024

Image source: G42, published by The National

The most recent choice of sides took place in the Middle East.

In 2023, US intelligence raised concerns about the relationship between Abu Dhabi AI company G42 and China. In December, G42 CEO Peng Xiao told the Financial Times, "We can't do both." G42 subsequently stopped using Huawei equipment and sold its investments in China, including its stake in ByteDance. In April 2024, Microsoft invested $1.5 billion in G42; withdrawing from China was a condition G42 had privately agreed upon with the US government before this investment. The middleman's business has always been about exploiting loopholes in the rules. The loophole of remote access has been visible to all parties for three years. BIS expressed concerns in its rule explanation in 2023, Nvidia conducted compliance reviews of each cloud partner, and bank loan documents listed the tenants. Nvidia also stated in March of this year that the export rules "by design" allowed cloud deployment outside regulated countries. The new rules on November 16th closed this loophole. A new round of siding with different sides has begun. Aolani's CEO said that about half of the contracted amount now comes from Western clients. According to the Straits Times, four of DayOne's top five clients are not Asian companies. The B300, originally leased to Chinese clients, is being relisted for sale to American and Western European buyers. Nvidia, on the other hand, turned around even earlier, telling its partners two weeks before the new regulations were released that Chinese clients would account for up to 49%. In the first three quarters of this year, data centers and cloud computing accounted for 35% of the approved investments in Malaysia. It has already chosen sides once. In May 2025, a deputy minister announced the use of Huawei's Ascend chips to build national-level AI infrastructure. Just a week earlier, the US Department of Commerce stated that using Ascend anywhere in the world could violate US export controls. The next day, the Deputy Minister's office retracted the statement, with Anwar saying the announcement was "premature." Two months later, Malaysia began requiring licenses for the export and transshipment of US AI chips. Regarding the new regulations, Malaysian Minister of International Trade and Industry Johari said, "If you want to stay at the table, you have to follow the US rules." Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong stated, "We don't enforce US export controls, but we don't want Singapore to be used or abused as a conduit." Middlemen can choose sides, but ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent cannot. There are 82 days left until the license expiry date of February 17, 2027.

data.title: What exactly are we expecting when we anticipate a bull market?
data.description:
Author: Blockchain Knight, Source: X, @BlocKnight21

There's an interesting change in the crypto market. In the past few years, people were always shouting that a bull market was coming, but now,

more and more people are starting to wonder when the bull market will actually arrive?

This feeling is even more pronounced in the altcoin market. Bitcoin continues to break price records, but many altcoins have yet to recover.

So

What exactly are we expecting in a bull market?

Is it a general market rise, with all our assets increasing in value?

Is it the expectation of a repeat of the bull market, where simply buying any project can yield several times the return? Or is it the anticipation of a market brimming with opportunities, allowing you to seize a chance to change your wealth? Upon closer examination, these expectations may ultimately point to the same thing: what we miss isn't the bull market itself, but the joy of making money within it. However, the problem is that a bull market doesn't guarantee profits for everyone; it can even be the beginning of losses for many. When a market rally begins, early entrants reap the rewards, and the profit-making effect attracts more capital. As prices rise, market sentiment becomes increasingly optimistic, and previously ignored projects begin to gain popularity. Later, many people stop caring about the projects themselves and only worry about missing the next surge (FOMO). At this point, early entrants begin to cash in their profits, while latecomers continue to chase higher prices; the more bustling the bull market, the easier it is to overlook the risks. A 2023 study by BIS found that before and after the Luna crash and FTX bankruptcy, large investors tended to sell, while small investors were more likely to buy. This illustrates that a market upturn does not guarantee profits for everyone; a bull market offers opportunities, not a guarantee of returns. In a bear market, accounts shrink, holdings decline, and once-favored projects go unnoticed. Over time, people easily doubt their judgments and even question the future of the industry. A bull market, on the other hand, brings the opposite: accounts start to profit, social media buzz returns, past judgments seem validated, and people regain a sense of control. However, this happiness is often short-lived, as desires rise with increasing profits. Therefore, bull markets offer more of a peak experience than lasting happiness. After the bull market ends, people will start waiting for the next bull market, hoping for a similar period of joy. Instead of pinning their hopes on bull markets, it's better to focus on bear markets. What's truly worthwhile in a bear market isn't guessing where the bottom is every day, but rather **re-understanding the market:** Which sectors still have growth potential? Which projects still have real business? Which assets are worth long-term attention? True investing is a bit like farming: sow in spring, harvest in autumn. No one can guarantee that every seed will bear fruit, but if you don't sow, you won't reap in autumn. Patience is the key to a bear market, while determination is the shield in a bull market. Patience allows you to maintain focus and judgment even when there's no profit-making opportunity, while determination allows you to execute your plan even when everyone else becomes greedy. We can look forward to a bull market, but we shouldn't make it our everything. After all, bull markets always end, and only the profits we actually realize truly belong to us.

data.title: Meta Refuses Pre-Launch Sandbox Test for Muse AI Agent After Giving the FCA Only Weeks of Notice
data.description:
Meta’s launch of its AI shopping assistant Muse in the UK has raised questions about how technology companies should be regulated when their products can act independently on behalf of consumers.

The debate intensified after Meta declined an offer from the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to jointly test Muse through its regulatory sandbox, leaving the watchdog to monitor the product after its public release.

Why Did Meta Reject The FCA’s Offer To Test Muse?

Colin Payne, head of innovation at the FCA, said Meta turned down the regulator’s proposal to test Muse under its supervision.

Speaking at a panel hosted by AI technology firm Whitespace on 24 November 2026, Payne said the FCA wanted to understand how autonomous AI agents interact with consumers, particularly when handling payments.

He said,

“We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market.”

Meta only informed the regulator of its UK launch plans in October, leaving little time to arrange testing, which typically requires weeks or months of preparation.

Meta spokesperson Matthew Pollard disputed the suggestion that the company had avoided regulatory engagement, saying:

“We've engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so.”

What Can Meta’s Muse AI Agent Do In The UK?

Muse became available to UK consumers on 24 November 2026 through iOS, Android, WhatsApp and its website.

Powered by Meta’s Muse Spark AI model, the assistant can handle everyday tasks such as online shopping, booking travel, renewing car insurance and requesting refunds.

Its UK launch partners include Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, ASOS, Currys, easyJet and Jet2.

Meta launched Muse in the UK today. This is just a short post to serve as a warning to people who might install this piece of spyware, as I have a lot of censorship and surveillance related posts in my drafts folder.

Meta is using Muse to build detailed dossiers on people. These…

— Paul Walsh (@Paul__Walsh) November 24, 2026

However, the British version has fewer financial capabilities than its US counterpart.

It cannot directly access bank accounts or provide personalised financial advice, although Meta has expressed interest in connecting Muse to UK banking services in the future, subject to regulatory approval and licensing.

For purchases, Muse uses Onelink, a digital wallet developed by Stripe that generates a digital version of a customer's payment card. Users can also check out through Shopify's Shop Pay at participating retailers.

Meta says users remain in control, as Muse must obtain permission before making purchases or sending emails. The assistant cannot access users' passwords or card details, and its activities can be reviewed.

Despite these safeguards, the FCA remains concerned about how autonomous systems could affect consumers.

Payne said,

“If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it's in the interest of the consumer.”

FCA Warns AI Agents Could Require Financial Licences

On the day Muse launched, the FCA published guidance warning that certain activities performed by AI agents could fall under existing financial regulations.

Four categories may require regulatory authorisation, including executing transactions, moving money, arranging borrowing and making investment decisions.

The regulator warned that companies offering regulated financial services without the necessary approval could face enforcement action, regardless of how they describe their products.

The FCA just drew the line for AI agents at what they do, not what they're called. Its new page says agents are moving beyond information to "initiating transactions, moving money, arranging borrowing or making investment decisions", and firms must understand which activities… https://t.co/bGwKozhP1H

— Chris Couch (@chriscouch) November 24, 2026

To examine how existing laws apply to autonomous AI systems, the FCA will bring together policymakers, financial institutions and technology providers through its Agentic Policy Sprint.

Other UK watchdogs have also raised concerns. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) stressed that consumers must understand how Muse handles their personal data and retain control over it.

Meanwhile, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) required Meta to revise its UK terms and conditions following discussions.

The updated terms require the company to exercise reasonable skill and care when providing the service, while acknowledging that AI responses may be inaccurate and tasks may not always be completed as intended.

Millions Already Use AI Agents As Regulators Struggle To Catch Up

The FCA's concerns come as consumer adoption of AI assistants continues to grow.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during the company's 21 October earnings call that more than 10 million people in the US and Canada had set up Muse within roughly six weeks of its September launch.

Around a quarter used the assistant on any given day.

Meta ($META) drove Muse daily downloads to a record 600k on Nov. 22 as international expansion pushed the assistant to top App Store rankings ahead of ChatGPT and Gemini. Per Sensor Tower data, Muse reached the #1 most downloaded free app ranking on Apple's App Store in Canada,… pic.twitter.com/bV3WjQF3k8

— 456X (@OptionKing666) November 26, 2026

A McKinsey report published on 28 October, based on a survey of approximately 21,000 consumers across 11 markets, found that 61% had used consumer AI tools and 53% had used AI for shopping.

Among AI users, 14% had completed purchases through AI.

Who wins when AI does the shopping?

data.title: GPT-6 Astra's sprint towards a grand unification theory is even more groundbreaking than the Riemann Hypothesis.
data.description:
The physics and AI communities were simultaneously shaken today. Stanford physicist Venkatesa Chandrasekaran released a groundbreaking 83-page paper on arXiv—"The Algebraic Quantumization of Gravity Starting from the Light Cone." It aims at the "holy grail" of physics that has been suspended for a century, trapping Einstein in his later years: non-perturbative quantum gravity in four-dimensional Lorentz spacetime. The core derivation and proof of the entire research were interactively deduced by Venkatesa and GPT-6 Astra, costing 400 million tokens. Ultraman excitedly retweeted, expressing his gratitude to OpenAI for having such talented individuals who could solve such a significant problem. OpenAI President Brockman highly praised it, saying it's "a step towards a deeper understanding of the universe." Einstein searched for 30 years, but one of the four fundamental forces was missing. There are four known fundamental forces in the universe. Electromagnetism, the strong force, and the weak force were all incorporated into quantum mechanics in the last century. But gravity remained, refusing to be included. Einstein spent the latter half of his life searching for a theory to unify them, but unfortunately, he never found one before his death. Later, we called this the "Grand Unification," and gravity was the final missing piece of the puzzle. Where does the real problem lie? Anyone who has studied quantum field theory knows that when dealing with gravity using the old methods, once the calculations reach the extremely microscopic scale, the equations explode with a bunch of infinity that cannot be eliminated, and the entire calculation goes out of control. In physics jargon, this is called "gravitational non-renormalization." Later string theory and loop quantum gravity, while each opening up new paths, also got stuck halfway through. In his paper, Venkatesa deviated from the conventional approach, directly addressing the "subjectivity of general relativity." He divided spacetime into countless "causal diamonds." Draw a light cone from a point in the past into the future, then draw another light cone from a point in the future into the past. Interlock the two cones mouth-to-mouth; the resulting rhomboid region is the space between them. He wrote all the gravitational information on the surface of the light cones, first quantizing them on the surface, and finally, like patchwork, sewing these rhomboid pieces back together along the edges to form a complete spacetime. Turning to the acknowledgments at the end of the paper, the tone suddenly shifts: Several hardcore derivations and proofs in the paper were painstakingly crafted by him over several months with GPT-6 Astra, resulting in a token loss of 400 million. At the very end of the acknowledgments list, Sam Altman's name is prominently displayed.

Looking back at Einstein, calculating forward to Hawking

To prove he wasn't just talking theory, Ven posed three questions to this theory.

The first question confronts infinity. What is the amplitude of the process when a pair of gravitons emerges from a light cone and then instantly annihilates? Following the usual procedure, we first expand using Newton's constant, then calculate term by term, resulting in a "logarithmic divergence"—the value increases with each subsequent calculation, heading directly towards infinity. Therefore, Ven changed the calculation order: first, we added all possible cases together, and then looked at the result. The second approach went straight to Hawking's black hole theory. In the 1970s, Bekenstein and Hawking pointed out that the entropy of a black hole is proportional to the area of ​​its event horizon. Starting from this light cone framework, the author first derived the famous Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of black holes, that is, how much information a black hole can hold at most. Next, he calculated a further layer of quantum correction to this black hole entropy, namely the single-loop logarithmic correction coefficient, which is exactly 10⁶/45. Interestingly, back in 2013, physicist Ashoke Sen calculated the same coefficient using Euclidean path integrals, also resulting in 10⁶/45. One path starts from the surface of the light cone, and the other follows the path integral; these two completely unrelated routes ultimately reach the same destination. The third path leads back to Einstein. Can this new theory, by lowering the energy, reconnect with the classical gravity we are familiar with? The paper provides a straightforward answer: yes. At the low-energy limit, it can logically derive a semi-classical Einstein equation with a series of quantum corrections. One person, one model, several months of work, overcoming three major hurdles—the paper claimed to have passed all three. That same evening, a group of Claudes came to grade the papers. Jonathan Oppenheim of University College London wrote an article overnight titled "Has AI Overturned Quantum Gravity?" His conclusion was: the paper's claims are completely untenable! It's too far removed from the true theory of quantum gravity! In his opening sentence, he poured cold water on the idea: "It's mostly only a matter of time before AI comes to steal quantum gravity. But dear readers, not today." He read the paper through himself and then called in a group of Claudes as reviewers. The Claudes first compiled a list of 21 known difficulties on this path, and then used this paper to check them one by one. Finally, he discovered that of the 21 known obstacles to the true theory of quantum gravity, the paper only solved one minor problem, bypassed seven, dropped six assumptions, and didn't mention the other seven at all. If you look further at Oppenheim's "three quick checks," you'll find that two of them directly refute the paper's most impressive conclusion. Didn't the paper claim to have calculated Hawking's black hole entropy? He directly points out that "it didn't count the microstates," using the old analytical extension argumentation approach. Didn't they claim to be able to derive Einstein's equations? He pointed out the flaw incisively: "The Hamiltonian operator relied upon in the proof was never actually created in the paper." As for the third question, it tested the core symmetry of general relativity—the invariance of differential homeomorphism. The paper failed to prove it from the ground up, instead using it directly as a ready-made axiom. His final judgment was: "This is a serious paper written by a serious physicist," but it is still far from a true theory of quantum gravity. Moreover, Geoff Penington, a leading scholar in quantum gravity at UC Berkeley, also questioned: "I have failed to find any part of the fundamental construct whose properties do not apply to non-renormalizable scalar field theory (because such a theory does not exist as a continuous quantum theory)." It seems that we are still some distance from a complete overturning of quantum gravity theory. AI's First Attempt to Find the "Ultimate Answer" in Physics You surely remember that scene in *The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy*: Humans built a computer called "Deep Thought" and asked it what the ultimate answer to life, the universe, and everything was. It calculated for 7.5 million years and gave a number: 42. No one can say for sure if this answer is correct, because no one can understand what the question is. The events in the AI ​​world these past few days have been almost identical stories. One machine spent months working with a human, burning through 400 million tokens, and delivered a report card on achieving unification; another company's group of machines determined the outcome in a single night. Human physicists, meanwhile, simply watched the AI ​​work. How many steps away from unification? Ultimately, this paper only quantizes pure gravity in a four-dimensional vacuum. Electrons and quarks haven't been included yet, and the other three forces haven't been connected either. Furthermore, it's only a preprint and hasn't undergone peer review; the acknowledgments of Maldacena, Strominger, and Penington only indicate they discussed and reviewed the manuscript, not that they endorsed it. OpenAI's Roon himself stated that theoretical physics, unlike mathematics, only has a portion that can be formally verified; whether it truly describes nature cannot be proven in a paper. Therefore, whether the paper has successfully proven anything remains inconclusive. Next, the world's top physicists will naturally examine this 83-page paper. This time, will you believe GPT-6 or Claude?

data.title: South Korea's draft Digital Assets Basic Law: How will the market be reshaped?
data.description:
Author: Eren, 100y; Source:FouFour Pillars; Compiled by: Shaw, Jinse Finance

Key Points

  • South Korea's proposed "Basic Law on Digital Assets" breaks through the existing regulatory framework centered on user protection and defines the business activities and responsibilities of the entire industry.

    • The bill replaces the existing Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) filing system with an activity-based licensing and registration framework, covering businesses such as trading, brokerage, custody, and investment management, laying the foundation for the development of over-the-counter trading, custody, and institutional brokerage. The issuance of won-denominated stablecoins will initially allow bank-led consortia to participate, with fintech companies allowed to join as the single largest shareholder. Foreign issuers must establish local offices, register with the Financial Services Commission (FSC), retain a portion of their reserve assets domestically, and submit token-related reports. This may limit the circulation of foreign stablecoins that struggle to meet these requirements domestically. To encourage traditional financial institutions to enter the digital asset industry, the bill introduces specific provisions to simplify the licensing application process for trust companies. This will also help support the development of domestic spot ETF custody infrastructure, potentially driving the digital asset financial services market, including custody and brokerage services, towards traditional financial institutions. Trading will be subject to pre- and post-listing disclosure obligations, with a 20% shareholding cap generally applied. Since the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) of Korea can suspend or prohibit the listing and trading of tokens with insufficient disclosure, overseas projects listed on Korean exchanges should prioritize disclosing information related to airdrops, token burns, and changes in circulating supply, while maintaining continuous communication with the exchanges. Licensed digital asset trading service providers will be allowed to provide liquidity according to contractual arrangements. While this introduces foreign market makers to the Korean market, commercial sustainability remains a separate issue requiring consideration, given licensing and compliance costs, market access in the Korean won, and foreign exchange regulations. The bill adds a new category for digital asset advisory services, requiring paid investment information services and paid referral activities to fulfill registration obligations. Two-way communication of investment-related opinions with paid subscribers may require registration as an investment management service provider. Referral activities for foreign exchange businesses that have not obtained the required Korean license or completed registration will also be prohibited. Regarding user protection, the bill imposes requirements on financial institutions regarding internal controls and information technology security, and introduces a no-fault liability system for losses caused by hacking attacks and information technology incidents. Violations of information technology security requirements can also result in punitive fines of up to 10% of revenue, increasing the security and risk management burden on service providers. The Basic Law marks the beginning, not the end, of the industry's institutionalization. For newly approved businesses to translate into substantial industry growth, market access for companies and foreign investors must be expanded, policies differentiating between traditional finance and digital assets must be reconsidered, and the Korean Won account and foreign exchange framework must be improved. The key lies in whether subsequent legislative processes and implementing laws can truly reflect actual business conditions.

1. South Korea's Basic Law on Digital Assets Officially Promulgated After More Than Three Years

The Financial Services Commission (FSC) of South Korea convened a meeting of its Virtual Assets Committee on November 24, 2026, and the Digital Assets Bill was formally submitted on November 26.

South Korea's regulation of virtual assets began with the introduction of a registration system for Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs) in the revised Act on Reporting and Use of Specific Financial Transaction Information, which came into effect in March 2021. The Virtual Assets User Protection Act, which came into effect in July 2024, marked the completion of the first phase of legislation.

The Digital Assets Act, enacted approximately three years and five months after the first phase of legislation passed by the National Assembly, is the second phase of legislation. Its regulatory scope extends beyond user protection, covering entry requirements, business activities, and the issuance and circulation of digital assets. As major economies continue to refine their regulatory frameworks, the South Korean digital asset industry has been awaiting the enactment of the Basic Law. In 2026, South Korea had approximately 11.18 million trading accounts, with first-half trading volume reaching approximately $360 billion, indicating extremely high market activity. From a market size perspective, the slow pace of regulatory development is disappointing. Recent market sentiment has been particularly weak, with first-half trading volume down 44% from approximately $646 billion in the first half of the year. This announcement is especially welcome given the South Korean digital asset industry's urgent need for new business and new sources of demand. This article primarily focuses on overseas solutions. Major South Korean financial institutions already interested in digital asset business may have already gained a deeper understanding of the Basic Law and its practical business impact through their own business assessments. Therefore, projects intending to enter the South Korean market or whose tokens are already listed on South Korean exchanges are likely to benefit more from this article. 2. What's Coming About Change: From "Virtual" Assets to Real-World Industries What changes will occur once this bill takes effect? ​​The government's proposal aims to reduce uncertainty in the digital asset industry and lay a regulatory foundation for the development of startups. South Korea's vague digital asset regulations have long been an obstacle to business expansion. There was no framework for issuing stablecoins denominated in Korean won at the time, and initial coin offerings (ICOs) have been banned domestically since 2017. Providing liquidity carries the risk of being classified as market manipulation, while restrictions on corporate trading accounts hinder institutional demand from entering the market. The lack of a dedicated regulatory framework for over-the-counter trading, custody, and investment management has made exchanges virtually the only viable business model in the South Korean digital asset industry. The government's proposal aims to broaden this previously niche industry. The first significant change is in terminology. The proposal replaces the legal term "virtual assets" with "digital assets." The Financial Services Commission (FSC) of Korea explained that this adjustment aims to strengthen alignment with global regulatory frameworks. Considering that the term "virtual" gives the impression of assets lacking substantial content and further reinforces their speculative nature, this adjustment can be understood as the government's attempt to change public perception of the industry. Beyond terminology, the way businesses are regulated is also changing. The government's proposal categorizes digital asset businesses by their activities and clarifies the scope of business and obligations for each service provider. Previously, different businesses were regulated under a single Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) registration framework. This resulted in regulatory costs comparable to those of financial institutions, while the scope of new businesses and their associated responsibilities were often unclear. To address this issue, the government's proposal establishes clear standards for the entry requirements, operating activities, and responsibilities of various businesses. For example, the proposal divides businesses into four categories: trading, brokerage, custody, and investment management, and sets rules for the issuance of stablecoins denominated in Korean won. Domestic token sales will also be permitted, provided disclosure procedures are followed. Simultaneously, as business opportunities continue to expand, the proposal further strengthens the regulation of business conduct and internal control requirements. Below, we will examine in detail the following six key changes: (1) Stablecoin issuance, (2) Licensing and registration based on business activities, (3) Domestic initial coin offerings and issuance disclosure, (4) Trading platform operation and circulation disclosure, (5) Liquidity provision, and (6) User protection. For those who find the detailed explanations too lengthy or complex, we believe that overseas companies and related agreements should focus on the following: Overseas Stablecoin Issuers: For overseas stablecoins such as USDT currently circulating on Korean exchanges, in order to maintain their listing status, issuers must meet regulatory requirements, including establishing branches or offices in Korea, depositing some reserve assets with Korean financial institutions, registering with the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) of Korea, and submitting filing reports for individual tokens. Just as USDT faced delisting and trading restrictions from major European exchanges after the implementation of the Crypto Asset Markets Regulation (MiCA), overseas stablecoins that do not meet South Korean regulatory requirements may also be delisted from the South Korean market. Unlike fiat-backed stablecoins issued by centralized issuers, decentralized and synthetic stablecoins with unclear issuers or opaque on-chain reserve management may struggle to meet these requirements, further limiting their listing and circulation on exchanges in the strictly regulated South Korean market. Token projects listed on South Korean exchanges: To obtain or maintain listing status on South Korean exchanges, projects must fully disclose required information, including total issuance, circulating supply, project status, and risk factors. Large transactions by the issuer, airdrops and burns that significantly impact the circulating supply, core technology changes, and hacking incidents also require temporary disclosure obligations, making continuous information sharing and communication with South Korean exchanges increasingly important. In particular, if a white paper or listing report contains material misrepresentations or omissions, the Financial Services Commission (FSC) of Korea can order rectification and, if necessary, directly suspend or prohibit the listing and trading of the relevant tokens. Since disclosure obligations also apply to listed projects, projects unable to provide sufficient information or maintain continuous disclosure capabilities face the risk of large-scale delisting. Foreign Spot and Futures Exchanges: Foreign exchanges already face operational restrictions in Korea, and market access may become even more difficult. Operating a spot exchange requires obtaining multiple digital asset business licenses and being designated as a platform operator by the Financial Supervisory Commission, which constitutes a significant barrier for foreign exchanges that have not yet established an entry path, such as acquiring existing Korean exchanges. Promotional regulations will also be further tightened. Companies that provide promotional services to foreign exchanges and receive compensation must register as digital asset consulting service providers. Even after registration, they are prohibited from providing promotional services to foreign exchanges that have not obtained a legal license or registration in Korea. Therefore, existing strategies in Korea for acquiring users through promotion are likely to face strict restrictions. Foreign Market Makers: This bill lays the regulatory foundation for foreign market makers to enter the South Korean market by allowing contractual liquidity provision. However, to operate in South Korea, a domestic branch or business office and a digital asset trading license are required. Therefore, meeting regulatory requirements regarding equity, personnel, and internal controls can be costly and time-consuming. Market access to the Korean won and foreign exchange regulations must also be considered. Foreign market makers need to assess South Korea's trading volume, liquidity provision needs, and whether expected returns can cover market entry and compliance costs. Foreign Custody Institutions: Foreign custody service providers must establish a domestic branch or business office in South Korea and obtain a digital asset custody license to provide custody services in South Korea. Global custody service provider BitGo has established an entity in South Korea with investments from Hana Financial Group and SK Telecom and completed its Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) registration in August 2026. Establishing local business premises and obtaining the necessary licenses are crucial for capitalizing on the increased participation of South Korean institutions and the early custody demand arising from the launch of spot ETFs. However, given the special regulations simplifying the custody license application process for existing financial institutions, overseas custody institutions should also consider strategies for competing with and cooperating with South Korean financial institutions. Paid Subscription Channels: Companies that provide digital asset valuation or investment decision advice to the public and charge fees must register as digital asset advisory service providers. Providing two-way investment-related communication or personalized advice to paid subscribers may require registration as an investment management service provider. However, the regulatory burden may be relatively low for overseas-operated paid subscription channels or research platforms targeting global clients that are accessed and subscribed to by South Korean users. Conversely, companies targeting the South Korean market with Korean-language content, advertising to domestic users, or recruiting paid South Korean subscribers should assess their domestic filing or registration obligations.

3. Key Changes Across Industries

3.1 Stablecoins: Initially Only Allowed for Issuance by Bank-Led Consortia

3.1.1 Details

The government's proposal established requirements for stablecoin issuance and user protection standards. Its legal terminology is "digital payment token," referring to digital assets pegged to a single currency and primarily used as a payment instrument.

The government's proposal established requirements for stablecoin issuance and user protection standards. Its legal terminology is "digital payment token," referring to digital assets pegged to a single currency and primarily used as a payment instrument.

The core terms are summarized below: **Initial Issuance Limited to Bank Consortia:** Participating banks must collectively hold a majority stake, while fintech companies or technology companies may be the single largest shareholder. **Domestic Registration and Token Filing for Foreign Issuers:** Foreign stablecoin issuers must establish a domestic office, register with the Financial Services Commission, and submit relevant reports through that office. They must also maintain a minimum amount of operating capital in Korea and deposit or entrust a portion of their reserve assets to domestic reserve asset managers such as banks. **Prohibition of Rewards:** Issuers, specific affiliates, and digital asset service providers are prohibited from providing economic benefits linked to the holding period. Exceptions, such as benefits related to transactions, will be specified by presidential decree. **Reserve Asset Requirements:** Reserve assets equivalent to or exceeding the outstanding issuance amount must be deposited or entrusted to institutions such as banks for custody. Reserve assets must be invested in highly liquid assets, such as deposits and government bonds denominated in linked currencies. **Important Token Designation:** Tokens with an outstanding balance of at least 1 trillion won can be designated based on their impact and will be subject to enhanced regulation. These tokens are subject to additional capital and liquidity management requirements, as well as information inquiries and joint inspections by the Bank of Korea. **Issuers must meet the minimum equity capital requirement of 5 billion won and the shareholder composition requirements stipulated by presidential decree to obtain approval from the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC). Initially, participating banks must collectively hold more than 50% of the shares; however, fintech companies or technology enterprises can be the single largest shareholder. It is worth noting that the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) clarified the launch sequence and explained that initial participation will be limited to banking consortia to ensure stable operation in the early stages, including compliance with regulatory requirements and anti-money laundering regulations. The licensing process for issuers and the approval for issuing stablecoins are independent processes. Licensed issuers must submit an issuance plan, covering the issuance period and limits, allocation methods, reserve asset management, and redemption scheme, for approval by the Financial Services Commission (FSC). Any significant changes to the approved plan require resubmission for approval. Reserve assets with a value at least 100% of the outstanding issuance amount must be deposited or held in custody with banks or other institutions and invested in highly liquid assets, including deposits denominated in linked currencies and government bonds. According to the FSC's proposed standards, US Treasury bonds therefore do not qualify as reserve assets for the Korean won stablecoin. The holding of reserve assets and the redemption process must always be publicly disclosed, and monthly audits of reserve assets and the submission of business reports are required. Stablecoin holders have the right to redeem their tokens at par value. Issuers should immediately redeem the tokens in equivalent currency upon the holder's request and may designate a redemption agent to assist with the process. However, issuers, related parties, and digital asset service providers are prohibited from directly or indirectly providing monetary or economic benefits linked to the holding period. Exceptions, such as benefits related to transactions, may be clarified by presidential decree. The Financial Services Commission (FSC) of Korea may designate tokens with an issuance amount of at least 1 trillion won as "significant digital payment tokens," taking into account factors such as the number of users, the token's impact on financial stability, and monetary policy. Reaching the 1 trillion won threshold does not automatically qualify a token as such. Issuers of designated tokens must maintain additional equity capital and strengthen reserve asset liquidity management, risk assessment, and the construction of a risk management framework. Foreign issuers seeking to provide issuance and redemption services to South Korean residents must establish a domestic branch or office in South Korea and register with the Financial Services Commission (FSC). The registration review committee assesses user protection arrangements, including adequate home-country regulation, South Korean resident representation, operating funds, and reserve asset management agreements. Foreign issuers must also deposit or entrust a portion of their reserve assets to a domestic reserve asset manager, such as the Bank of Korea. The amount of reserve assets to be held domestically will be determined by presidential decree, taking into account the home-country regulatory framework and the holdings and circulation of stablecoins in South Korea. Registered domestic offices must submit separate reports for the foreign stablecoins they intend to handle in South Korea. Only stablecoins whose submitted documents are approved can be listed and traded on Korean exchanges. This practice is similar to the EU's Crypto-Asset Markets Regulation (MiCA). The MiCA also requires stablecoin issuers to obtain authorization within the EU, submit a white paper, and deposit a certain percentage of their reserve assets with financial institutions, while prohibiting the listing of stablecoins that do not meet regulatory requirements.

3.1.2 Commentary

A notable feature of South Korea's stablecoin bill is that it classifies fintech companies as a separate participating category, allowing them to become the single largest shareholder, while banks collectively hold a majority stake. The South Korean government's example proposal involves four banks each holding 15%, totaling 60%, and one fintech company holding 30%.

However, becoming the largest shareholder does not necessarily guarantee managerial control. If the banks collectively exercise their voting rights, their votes can exceed those of the fintech company. Therefore, actual control depends on the board composition, voting requirements, and the power to appoint executives. Even if a fintech company leads technology development and business operations, every major decision requires approval from multiple banks, which could slow down business execution.

Therefore, the actual business structure will depend on the internal dynamics among alliance members and cannot be predicted solely from the government's proposal. The proposal only establishes a broad issuance framework.

Whether banks are responsible for managing reserves and compliance, fintech companies for operational services, and how responsibilities for major decisions and event responses are divided will all depend on negotiations among alliance members. From a business perspective, where initial demand will emerge remains to be seen. The Korean won stablecoin can be used in existing fintech retail payment networks and may initially replace some USDT, USDC, or Korean won deposits on exchanges and on-chain. However, given the significant differences in why users hold Korean won and US dollars, we expect demand for US dollar stablecoins will not directly translate into demand for Korean won stablecoins. Profitability largely depends on issuance size. Since reserve asset yields are the issuer's primary revenue source, distribution channels that can drive issuance growth are crucial. However, the bill prohibits not only issuers but also certain related parties and digital asset service providers from offering rewards tied to holding periods. Since exceptions to transaction-related benefits may be stipulated by presidential decree, the permitted scope of payment and transaction rewards will be a key variable in distribution strategies. JPYC has clearly demonstrated the relationship between rewards and the circulating supply of fiat-backed stablecoins. After decentralized finance (DeFi) service platform Unifi lowered its deposit yield from 5% to 2% in September, the circulating supply of JPYC dropped by more than a third within a week. Foreign issuers must also secure domestic distribution channels. In particular, they must meet new operational requirements. To offer issuance and redemption services in South Korea, they must establish a branch in South Korea based on authorization from their home country, register with the Financial Services Commission (FSC), and ensure they have a resident representative in South Korea, operating funds, and user protection arrangements. Tokens issued overseas also require separate registration for circulation in South Korea. Once the Basic Law comes into effect, foreign stablecoin issuers currently listed on South Korean exchanges are expected to lose their eligibility for domestic circulation if they fail to establish local business operations and register with the FSC. Another point of concern is how Korean won stablecoins will interact with other forms of digital won as domestic and foreign issuers compete. The Bank of Korea has consistently argued that central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) and bank-issued deposit tokens should form the core of digital currency, with stablecoins playing a supplementary role. However, if fintech companies rapidly expand the use of stablecoins using their existing user networks, bank-led initiatives could become mere formalities within the government framework. Another viable model is for deposit tokens and CBDCs to be used for interbank and cross-border payments, while private stablecoins serve personal retail payments. While the government's proposal establishes a framework for issuance, the actual form of currency used and the scenarios in which it will be implemented will depend on the services offered by banks and fintech companies.

3.2 Digital Asset Business: Introduction of an Activity-Based Licensing and Registration System

3.2.1 Details

The current regulatory framework for Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs) in South Korea is centered on the registration system under the Act on Reporting and Use of Specific Financial Transaction Information.

Virtual asset service providers' businesses are categorized into five types: (a) buying and selling virtual assets, (b) exchanging virtual assets with other virtual assets, (c) transferring virtual assets, (d) custody and management of virtual assets, and (e) providing intermediary, arrangement, or facilitation services for transactions and exchanges. Under this framework, exchanges in the Korean won and cryptocurrency markets, over-the-counter trading service providers, custodians, and custodian wallet providers are required to register with the Financial Intelligence Service (FIU) of Korea before commencing operations. Key registration requirements include Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification and ensuring that deposit and withdrawal accounts for businesses handling Korean won transactions are verified with real names. The regulatory focus is on anti-money laundering and user protection. While various business activities are categorized, there is no separate licensing and registration framework or differentiated equity requirements for each business category, which distinguishes the current regulatory system from the business activity-based regulatory framework introduced in the Basic Law on Digital Assets. The Financial Supervisory Authority (FSA) will abolish the existing registration system for virtual asset service providers and categorize digital asset businesses into four types: trading, brokerage, custody, and investment management. Under a supplementary licensing model, companies can combine multiple services as needed. Trading: Companies use their own funds and assets to trade directly with users, typically through institutional over-the-counter trading desks or asset exchange services. This is similar to the role of market makers in traditional finance. Brokerage: Businesses that execute orders on behalf of users or connect buyers and sellers. Custody: Companies that safeguard and manage users' digital assets and private keys, and may optionally provide staking services. Investment Management: A business that manages clients' digital asset portfolios or provides investment advice. The difference between trading and brokerage lies in whose account the trade is conducted on. Trading service providers use their own funds and assets as counterparties to conduct business with users; institutional over-the-counter trading desks and asset exchange services are typical examples. In the overseas asset exchange model launched by the Financial Services Commission (FSC) of South Korea, when a user makes an asset exchange request, the service provider quotes a price including fees. If the user accepts the offer, the service provider directly sells or exchanges the asset. In contrast, brokerage service providers execute orders on behalf of users or connect buyers and sellers in the over-the-counter market. Brokerage businesses also allow over-the-counter trading, but unlike trading businesses, the provider's role is limited to intermediary. Exchanges that aggregate and competitively match orders from multiple users are classified separately. Holding only a brokerage license is insufficient to operate an exchange. Operators must obtain trading, brokerage, and custody licenses and be designated as platform operators by the Financial Supervisory Commission. Trading and brokerage service providers may also lend digital assets to clients. However, cash loans for trading are prohibited, and the eligible assets, client qualifications, collateral ratios, and loan terms will be determined by presidential decree. Custody refers to the business of holding and managing users' digital assets and private keys. Custodians must separate client assets from corporate assets and establish safeguards against events such as hacking. They may also provide staking services with client consent. Custodians may directly participate in verification or use external validators, but may not delegate clients' private keys to third parties. Investment management refers to the business of managing clients' digital asset portfolios or providing investment advice. It is worth noting that under the previous framework for virtual asset service providers, investment management was not a separate business category. For example, discretionary investment services that adjust Bitcoin and Ethereum allocations according to client-defined authorizations, or advisory services advising clients on which assets to hold and their proportions. However, this act generally prohibits pooling assets from multiple clients for collective investment. Therefore, the new investment management category formalizes discretionary investment and advisory services for digital assets, but does not immediately permit the establishment and operation of digital asset funds. Obtaining investment management registration alone does not allow direct custody of client assets or lending of funds and other assets. As mentioned earlier, exchanges are in a separate category. Obtaining trading, brokerage, and custody licenses does not automatically grant the right to operate an exchange. Operators must meet market operation requirements, including sufficient equity capital, market monitoring systems, and conflict-of-interest prevention mechanisms, and must be designated as a "digital asset platform operator" by the Financial Supervisory Commission. Finally, the proposal establishes standards for applying regulatory provisions to decentralized finance (DeFi). Transactions executed automatically through smart contracts without intermediaries are generally not classified as digital asset business activities. However, if an identifiable party can influence changes to the smart contract, the service may be subject to the regulations outlined in the presidential order. For example, if the operating team has the authority to upgrade the contract or modify trading conditions, automated execution alone does not exempt the service from regulation. The key is who actually controls the service, not whether it's labeled as decentralized finance (DeFi).

3.2.2 Commentary

South Korea's exchange-centric market will allow over-the-counter trading desks, brokerage firms, independent custodians, and market makers to operate as professional institutions. Integrating multiple licenses can also promote a prime brokerage model similar to Coinbase Prime, providing institutional clients with integrated services encompassing trading, custody, and investment management.

However, exchanges are subject to separate business restrictions. Even holding trading, brokerage, and custody licenses, exchanges are generally prohibited from acting as direct counterparties to clients outside their own market, nor from providing investment management services to their own clients. The market should not be dominated by exchanges providing all services; instead, it should develop around a division of roles among different trading, brokerage, and investment management service providers.

It's worth noting that South Korea has introduced special provisions to simplify market entry procedures for existing financial institutions.

Some trust companies established under the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act are considered to have obtained the relevant licenses simply by registering with the Financial Supervisory Service (FSC) when conducting digital asset business activities as stipulated by the Presidential Decree. Ordinary digital asset custodians must meet eight licensing application requirements, including equity capital, business plan feasibility, and qualifications of major shareholders and senior management; while qualified trust companies only need to meet three requirements: personnel and physical infrastructure, sound financial condition and social reputation, and conflict of interest prevention mechanisms. The review period has also been shortened from three months for standard license applications to two months for registration. By reducing the repetitive regulatory burden on financial institutions that have already completed qualification reviews in the existing licensing process, these provisions encourage banks and securities companies to enter the digital asset custody market, support the construction of custody infrastructure for future spot digital asset exchange-traded funds (ETFs), and promote prime brokerage services (PBS) for institutional investors. Specific qualification standards and permitted business activities will be determined by the Presidential Decree. The special provisions for trust companies are particularly relevant to the launch of domestic spot Bitcoin ETFs. The scope of eligible underlying assets stipulated in the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act, and the ability of trust companies to custody digital assets, have long been considered major legal obstacles to the domestic spot digital asset ETF market. This bill lays the regulatory foundation for addressing the latter issue by lowering the entry barrier for existing trust companies to directly provide digital asset custody services. However, these provisions themselves do not expand the scope of eligible underlying assets or trust property stipulated in the bill, meaning that separate legislative and regulatory adjustments are needed before the launch of spot ETFs.
